key_terms.meaning: An excited atom drops to a lower level on its own and emits a photon of energy hν; the direction and phase are random.
A photon of energy hν makes an excited atom drop and emit a second photon in the same mode, with the same phase, direction and wavelength.
Probability per unit time that an atom in level 2 emits spontaneously; unit s⁻¹.
Rates of absorption and stimulated emission per unit spectral energy density; A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³.
N₂ > N₁, so stimulated emission outnumbers absorption and the medium amplifies light.
Supplying energy by flash lamp, electric discharge or current to raise atoms to the upper laser level and hold the inversion.
Two mirrors around the gain medium that send light back and forth, build up intensity and select longitudinal modes.
An upper level with a long spontaneous lifetime (about 10⁻³ s), so atoms stay long enough to build an inversion.
A fixed phase relation between waves: temporal coherence (long coherence length) and spatial coherence (same phase across the beam).
Lasing ends on the ground level, so more than half the atoms must be pumped up; needs high pump power and usually runs pulsed.
Laser output that stays on steadily, as in the He-Ne laser, instead of giving short pulses.
Neodymium ions in a yttrium aluminium garnet crystal; four-level, pulsed or CW, main line at 1064 nm.
Electric discharge in CO₂, N₂ and He; a vibrational transition gives 10.6 μm infrared at high power.
Organic dye in a liquid solvent with a broad gain band, tuned over tens of nanometres by a grating or prism.
A semiconductor whose conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum lie at the same k, so electrons and holes recombine radiatively with high probability.
A forward-biased p-n junction with a Fabry-Perot cavity formed by cleaved facets; it lases when gain exceeds loss.
NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) = sin θ_a, where n₁ and n₂ are core and cladding indices and θ_a is the acceptance angle.
Light going from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle above the critical angle is reflected back completely.
Core refractive index falls smoothly from the axis to the cladding, so rays curve and arrive together, reducing dispersion.
α = (10/L) log₁₀(P_in/P_out), in dB per km, caused by absorption and scattering.

takeaways: An atom can give out light on its own (spontaneous) or be forced by a passing photon (stimulated); only stimulated emission gives amplification.
Einstein's A and B coefficients tie absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission together, and give A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³.
Laser action needs population inversion, a gain medium, pumping and an optical cavity with two mirrors.
Laser light is bright, coherent, directional and nearly monochromatic because of stimulated emission inside a resonator.
Ruby is a three-level pulsed laser; He-Ne is a four-level gas laser that runs continuously by resonant transfer from helium to neon.
The gain medium decides the wavelength: Nd:YAG gives 1064 nm, CO₂ gives 10.6 μm, dye lasers can be tuned widely.
A semiconductor laser uses injected carriers, a direct band gap and cleaved facets, so it is tiny, efficient and cheap.
An optical fibre guides light by total internal reflection in a core of higher refractive index than the cladding.
Refractive-index profile and core size decide step versus graded and single-mode versus multimode operation.
Attenuation and dispersion fix repeater spacing, and the same fibre can act as a sensor when light reacts to strain, temperature or current.
bank_note: Long answers are usually asked on the Einstein-coefficient relation, population inversion and pumping, construction and working of ruby, He-Ne or semiconductor lasers, characteristics of laser light, fibre structure and numerical aperture, and attenuation or link-budget numericals.

bank.q: Distinguish spontaneous and stimulated emission. Using the three rate equations for absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission, derive the relation A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³.
outline: Define both processes with energy-level diagrams
Write rates R_abs = B₁₂N₁ρ(ν), R_stim = B₂₁N₂ρ(ν), R_spon = A₂₁N₂
Set thermal equilibrium and use Planck's radiation law
Compare with Boltzmann ratio to get B₁₂ = B₂₁
Obtain A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³ and note the ν³ dependence

bank.q: Explain population inversion, pumping and the role of a metastable state. Why does a three-level laser need much more pump power than a four-level laser?
outline: Meaning of N₂ > N₁ and why it cannot occur in thermal equilibrium
Pumping schemes: optical, electrical, chemical
Metastable level and its long lifetime
Rate equations idea for three- and four-level systems
Three-level needs more than half of the atoms pumped; four-level ends on a nearly empty level

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of a ruby laser with an energy-level diagram. State why it is operated in pulses.
outline: Ruby = Al₂O₃ doped with about 0.05% Cr³⁺
Three levels: ground, pump bands, metastable level
Flash-lamp pumping, population inversion, stimulated emission at 694.3 nm
Silvered rod ends form the resonator
Pulsed because the lower laser level is the ground level and pumping must be repeated

bank.q: Describe the He-Ne laser. Explain resonant transfer of energy from helium to neon and why the output is continuous.
outline: Gas mixture ratio and pressure, discharge tube with Brewster windows and mirrors
Helium metastable levels near neon 3s and 2s levels
Collision transfers energy to neon; inversion on neon levels
Output lines at 632.8 nm, 1.15 μm, 3.39 μm
Four-level cycle ends on a fast-decaying level, so CW operation is possible

bank.q: List the characteristics of laser light and explain the physical reason for each: monochromaticity, coherence, directionality and brightness.
outline: Definition and measure of each property
Role of stimulated emission in phase and direction
Resonator selects frequency and direction
Brightness as power per unit area per unit solid angle
Typical numbers for a He-Ne or diode laser

bank.q: Calculate the ratio of stimulated to spontaneous emission rates for a transition at 600 nm at 300 K, and state what the result means for a lamp compared with a laser.
outline: Use R_stim/R_spon = (1/(e^{hν/kT} − 1)) type expression
Compute hν in eV and kT = 0.026 eV
Show the ratio is about 10⁻³⁵ at thermal equilibrium
Conclude that ordinary sources are dominated by spontaneous emission
Explain that population inversion, not temperature, makes the ratio large

bank.q: A step-index fibre has core index 1.50 and cladding index 1.48. Find the numerical aperture, the acceptance angle in air and the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary.
outline: NA = √(n₁² − n₂²)
Substitute to get NA ≈ 0.244
θ_a = sin⁻¹(NA) ≈ 14.1°
Critical angle θ_c = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁) ≈ 80.6°
Comment on how a larger index difference accepts more light but increases dispersion

bank.q: A 3 km fibre takes 1 mW input and gives 0.5 mW output. Find the attenuation in dB/km. If the system allows a 30 dB loss budget, estimate the maximum repeater spacing.
outline: Loss in dB = 10 log₁₀(P_in/P_out)
Obtain about 3.01 dB over 3 km
α ≈ 1.0 dB/km
Repeater spacing ≈ 30/1.0 = 30 km
Mention connector and splice losses reducing the practical figure

bank.q: A He-Ne laser gives 1 mW at 632.8 nm. Find the photon energy and the number of photons emitted per second.
outline: E = hc/λ in joules and eV
Number per second = P/hν
Answer near 3.2 × 10¹⁵ photons per second
Comment on why such a small power is still visually bright

bank.q: Choose a laser for (a) cutting a 5 mm steel sheet, (b) eye surgery, (c) a long-haul fibre link and (d) a supermarket barcode scanner. Justify each choice by wavelength, power and mode of operation.
outline: CO₂ at 10.6 μm for metal cutting: high power, strong absorption by metals
Pulsed visible or near-infrared laser for surgery: controlled pulse energy, low average heating
Semiconductor laser near 1.3 or 1.55 μm for fibre links: low attenuation window, direct modulation
Low-power diode laser for scanning: cheap, compact, safe power level
Match each case to wavelength, power, coherence and pulse length

bank.q: Compare ruby, Nd:YAG, He-Ne, CO₂ and semiconductor lasers on gain medium, wavelength, level scheme, mode of operation, power level and typical application.
outline: Table across all five lasers
Wavelength: 694.3 nm, 1064 nm, 632.8 nm, 10.6 μm, 0.8-1.6 μm
Level scheme: three-level ruby, four-level Nd:YAG and He-Ne, band-to-band diode
Pulsed versus CW and typical output powers
Link each to an application such as drilling, alignment, cutting, communication

bank.q: Explain why a semiconductor laser needs a direct band gap, heavy doping, forward bias and cleaved facets. Compare a laser diode with an LED.
outline: Direct gap gives radiative recombination; indirect gap gives heat
Heavy doping gives population inversion at moderate current
Forward bias injects carriers into the active region
Cleaved facets give about 30% feedback, forming the cavity
Threshold current, coherence and linewidth compared with LED

bank.q: Explain how attenuation and dispersion limit a fibre link. Compare step-index multimode, graded-index multimode and single-mode fibre, and select one for a 50 km link at 1.55 μm.
outline: Absorption and Rayleigh scattering set the attenuation window
Modal and material dispersion broaden pulses and limit bit rate
Ray paths and pulse spreading in each fibre type
Core size and NA values, single-mode condition
Choose single mode at 1.55 μm for long distance and high bit rate

bank.q: Discuss the use of lasers in industry, medicine, communication and sensing. Explain how coherence, pulse length and wavelength decide the choice, and state one safety precaution for each use.
outline: Welding, cutting, drilling: high power and good focus
Surgery and ophthalmology: selective absorption, short pulses
Fibre communication: modulation bandwidth and low-loss window
Sensors and measurement: coherence and interferometry
Eye and skin hazard, interlocks, protective goggles

glossary.def: Random emission of a photon when an excited atom falls to a lower level without any external light.
Emission forced by an incoming photon, giving a second photon identical in phase, direction and wavelength.
An excited state with an unusually long lifetime, used to store atoms before lasing.
A condition where more atoms sit in the upper laser level than in the lower one.
The process of supplying energy to create and maintain population inversion.
The material (solid, gas, liquid or semiconductor) that provides gain in a laser.
A pair of mirrors that reflects light through the gain medium many times and selects the lasing modes.
The distance over which a light wave keeps a predictable phase relation with itself.
Narrow spread of wavelengths in the output, measured by Δλ or Δν.
The property that laser light travels in a narrow beam with small divergence.
Power emitted per unit area per unit solid angle; lasers give very high values.
A laser whose lower lasing level is empty at room temperature, so the threshold pump power is low.
A laser that delivers energy in short bursts rather than continuously.
Laser output that remains on at a steady power.
A band gap in which electrons and holes recombine mainly by emitting photons.
A p-n junction laser in which injected carriers recombine and the cleaved ends form the cavity.
A thin glass or plastic thread that guides light along its core by total internal reflection.
The central light-carrying region of a fibre, with refractive index higher than the cladding.
The outer glass layer of lower refractive index that keeps light inside the core.
A plastic coating over the cladding that protects the fibre from mechanical damage.
The outermost protective cable sheath holding one or more buffered fibres.
The sine of the largest acceptance angle, giving the light-gathering ability of a fibre.
A ray that passes through the fibre axis after each reflection at the core-cladding boundary.
A fibre in which the refractive index changes abruptly from core to cladding.
A fibre in which the refractive index decreases smoothly across the core.
Loss of optical power along a fibre, quoted in decibels per kilometre.
